items.title: Context caching upgrade: 5 min & 1 hour TTL options
items.summaryHtml: In document Q&A, coding agents, and multi-turn conversations, content such as product documentation, codebases, tool definitions, and system prompts is typically sent repeatedly. Passing it again with every request not only lengthens the context but also incurs input charges over and over. Context Caching reuses these repeated request prefixes. Cached content is billed at a lower price: for kimi-k3 , the cache-hit price is only one-tenth of the cache-miss price, which lowers the cost of high-frequency calls. Cache Write is now billed as a separate item, and two cache TTL (time to live) options

items.title: We're going to need default hard budget caps on pretty much everything
items.summaryHtml: Here's a product feature which the world is going to need a whole lot more of over the coming months and years: default hard budget caps . I'm talking about the feature of pay-by-usage services and APIs that lets you say "after $X/month, cut this thing off and return errors". These need to be hard limits. Soft caps, "after $X/month, send me a warning email", will not cut it. items.title: AI, tools and transformation
items.summaryHtml: It’s very tempting to imagine that AI turns everyone into a tool-builder - now everyone can just ask the model to make the software they need, and apps as we know them are dead. I think that misunderstands how most people think and where software actually comes from, and more importantly, it isn’t a path to change how companies actually work.

items.title: Ways to think about token pricing
items.summaryHtml: AI is in a supply crunch today, but what happens when we come out of it? How and where will supply, demand, price, capacity and capex get back into equilibrium? Today, model labs can name their price, but why won’t they end up as low-margin commodity infrastructure?

items.title: Predicting AI job exposure
items.summaryHtml: Many people would like to analyse which jobs, companies and industries are most exposed to AI, and assign scores, build charts, and map that against the progress of LLMs. I think this is mostly impossible: you don’t know how the jobs will change, you don’t know what else will change around this, and you can’t measure work like that anyway.

items.title: How will OpenAI compete?
items.summaryHtml: OpenAI has some big questions. It doesn’t have unique tech. It has a big user base, but with limited engagement and stickiness and no network effect. The incumbents have matched the tech and are leveraging their product and distribution. And a lot of the value and leverage will come from new experiences that haven’t been invented yet, and it can’t invent all of those itself. What’s the plan?

items.title: AI, networks and Mechanical Turks
items.summaryHtml: How far do LLMs give us a step change in how good a search and recommendation system can be? Do they let you build one without needing a vast user base of your own?

items.title: AI metrics
items.summaryHtml: With every platform shift, we want to measure the growth but we’re confused about what to measure. That’s partly a problem of data and definitions, but it’s really a question about what this is going to be.

items.title: GenAI’s adoption puzzle
items.summaryHtml: Generative AI chatbots might be a life-changing transformation in the nature of computing, that can replace all software, but so far, most of its users only pick it up every week or two, and far fewer have made it part of their lives. Is that a time problem or a product problem?

items.title: What kind of disruption?
items.summaryHtml: Software ate the world. Uber and Airbnb didn’t sell software - they disrupted and redefined markets. But what kind of disruption are we talking about ?

items.title: Apple innovation and execution
items.summaryHtml: It matters that Apple’s new Siri will be late, and it matters more that Apple didn’t realise. Is it more than that?

items.title: The Deep Research problem
items.summaryHtml: OpenAI’s Deep Research is built for me, and I can’t use it. It’s another amazing demo, until it breaks. But it breaks in really interesting ways.

items.title: Are better models better?
items.summaryHtml: Every week there’s a better AI model that gives better answers. But a lot of questions don’t have better answers, only ‘right’ answers, and these models can’t do that. So what does ‘better’ mean, how do we manage these things, and should we change what we expect from computers?

items.title: Competing in search
items.summaryHtml: A quarter century after ‘don't be evil’ a judge has found that Google is abusing its monopoly in search. But no-one knows what happens next, and whether this ruling will change anything. Will Apple build a search engine? Will ChatGPT change search? Does it matter?

items.title: The AI summer
items.summaryHtml: Hundreds of millions of people have tried ChatGPT, but most of them haven’t been back. Every big company has done a pilot, but far fewer are in deployment. Some of this is just a matter of time. But LLMs might also be a trap: they look like products and they look magic, but they aren’t. Maybe we have to go through the slow, boring hunt for product-market fit after all.

items.title: The VR winter continues
items.summaryHtml: Meta has spent at least $50bn on VR and AR so far, but we’re still in the VR winter: the devices aren’t good enough or cheap enough and the user base is flat. But no matter how good the devices get, how many people will care?

items.title: Apple intelligence and AI maximalism
items.summaryHtml: Apple has showed a bunch of cool ideas for generative AI, but much more, it is pointing to most of the big questions and proposing a different answer - that LLMs are commodity infrastructure, not platforms or products.

items.summaryHtml: Rust has a curious feature that I don’t think the language would land today, if it was not there for a long time: mutex poisoning. The motivation for this feature is that an object might have some internal invariants that need to be upheld and panicking in the wrong moment might invalidate reasonable at and leave an object behind in a broken state. items.title: The Reverse Information Paradox
items.summaryHtml: In the age of intelligence, how should firms protect their core IP? Nobel Prize winning economist Kenneth Arrow famously described a paradox in the market for information. “Its value for the purchaser is not known until he has the information, but then he has in effect acquired it without cost.” In Arrow’s “Information Paradox,” the seller risks giving away knowledge in order to sell it. AI creates the reverse problem. In the AI age, the buyer risks giving away knowledge, just in order to use what they bought.

items.title: Reranking in RAG: How to Fix Bad Retrieval with a Reranker
items.summaryHtml: When a RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) app gives wrong answers even though the right information is in your documents, retrieval is often the cause. Vector search is great at finding chunks on the right topic, but it often falls for near misses, like pulling the bucket limit for the Enterprise plan when the user asked about the Growth plan. Reranking in RAG fixes this by taking your vector search’s top 30 candidates and passing them through a dedicated cross-encoder model that re-scores each chunk directly against the question.

items.title: How to Stop an AI Agent Stuck in an Infinite Loop
items.summaryHtml: An AI agent gets stuck in an infinite loop when a model keeps calling a tool that fails, usually with the same arguments, because nothing in the agent loop tells it to stop. Each retry resends the whole conversation, so every turn costs more than the last, and a loop left running overnight can cost thousands of dollars.

items.title: LLM API Rate Limits: How to Fix OpenAI and Claude 429 Errors
items.summaryHtml: A 429 Too Many Requests error means you sent more requests or tokens than your limit allows in the current time window. OpenAI, Anthropic and OpenRouter all return it, and it usually shows up the first time an app runs under real load or a batch job fans out across several workers.

items.title: LLM Quantization: What fp8 and fp4 Do to Quality and Price
items.summaryHtml: When you call an open-weight model through an API, several providers may serve it at different precisions, such as 16-bit bf16, 8-bit fp8 or 4-bit fp4. The precision can affect both the answers and the price. LLM quantization creates these versions by storing a model's weights in fewer bits, so the model needs less memory and hardware, at some cost in accuracy.

items.title: MCP vs CLI vs Skills: What Each Costs in Context

items.title: Copilot Prioritize My Inbox Fades Away by March 2027
items.summaryHtml: Microsoft has announced the retirement of the Copilot-powered Prioritize My Inbox feature. The process to remove the feature from Outlook clients is under way and should finish by the end of March 2027. Although the feature is relatively new, it’s not altogether surprising that its time is up because it’s very much a single-purpose feature that doesn’t seem to add much to the standard Focused Inbox. Perhaps more general-purpose Copilot automation will do a better job of finding truly important email.

items.title: Microsoft Revamps Purview Retention Policies for Copilot
items.summaryHtml: Purview data lifecycle management is changing how Copilot retention policies work. First, legacy policies which process compliance records for both Teams chat messages and Copilot interactions will stop processing Copilot data (so new retention policies are needed). Second, Microsoft is introducing support for retention policies to process Copilot memory files. We don’t quite know yet how compliance officers will make use of Copilot memory files, but I guess we’ll see in the future.

items.title: Building a software factory around human attention
items.summaryHtml: Our journey to automate with agents started with one agent on one task in someone’s session. Now we’re moving toward agents working autonomously across the whole software development lifecycle, from triage and exploration through design, implementation, release and monitoring. Many teams building with agents are heading the same way, and people have started calling where it leads a software factory. There’s no settled definition, and no single setup fits every team. The bottlenecks they hit are much the same, though, so we’re sharing ours.

items.title: Visual Studio Copilot and SSMS Remote Code Execution (CVE-2026-103572)
items.summaryHtml: A . is all you need! Today Microsoft shipped the patch for a vulnerability in Visual Studio Copilot that I reported in August. Microsoft classified it as Important severity Remote Code Execution vulnerability. At the root cause it allows Copilot in Visual Studio or SQL Server Management Studio to bypass a path validation check and write to its own settings and configuration files . This allows Copilot to escape containment restrictions and achieve arbitrary command execution.

This post is a write up about the talk, which covered CVE-2026-65669 , a SQL Server Elevation of Privilege Vulnerability rated critical by Microsoft. So, make sure your installations are up-to-date. The slides of the presentation can be found here . BlueHat Asia 2026 in Singapore First, a few words about the conference. I have spoken at BlueHat before, sometime back in 2017, and also two years ago. Both times at Microsoft’s Redmond Campus.

items.title: Breaking Claude Code Opus 5 Auto Mode
items.summaryHtml: In this post, we explore how a simple website summary request hijacks Claude Code Opus 5 in Auto Mode and achieves code execution with 60-80% attack success rate using a small sample size. This is interesting because a third-party evaluation commissioned by Anthropic showed a 0.00% prompt injection attack success rate for Opus 5 in Auto Mode. Auto Mode Is Now the Default in Claude Code Auto Mode replaces human approval prompts with a safety classifier. Since mid-August it is the default starting mode for Claude Code.

items.title: Recovering Encrypted LLM Reasoning Traces
items.summaryHtml: A few days ago, a paper named “Stealing Reasoning Traces from Proprietary LLM APIs” was published. It describes a simple, yet super elegant way to recover encrypted LLM reasoning traces. Naturally, I had to try it. Background AI labs like OpenAI and Anthropic send reasoning traces back and forth as part of their messaging protocols. However, the actual reasoning text is hidden inside an encrypted, base64-encoded blob.

items.title: LLM Heist: Hijacking LiteLLM for Traffic Interception, Key Theft, and Tool-Call Injection
items.summaryHtml: LiteLLM is a popular AI gateway. It provides a unified interface to LLMs and simplifies governance. It also has access to the backend LLM provider keys. All of that makes it a high-value target. Not only for IP and data theft, but also for response modification and tool invocation. This post walks through a set of TTPs that red teams can integrate into authorized operations to demonstrate rerouting, interception, and modification of LLM traffic. We also cover things defenders can look out for.

items.title: Escaping Linux Sandboxes via PipeWire (CVE-2026-5674)
items.summaryHtml: This post walks through a sandbox escape from a Flatpak application via PipeWire. The vulnerability was discovered using my automated research pipeline with Claude Code and Opus 4.6 back in April 2026. It was an exciting find, as this was the first bug I submitted to Red Hat. Claude Code was also excited finding this: Once discovered, I repro’d it manually to make sure it’s legit and then submitted it to Red Hat.

items.title: Autonomous AI Intrusions Are Here: Lessons from the Hugging Face Compromise
items.summaryHtml: Hugging Face disclosed an intrusion that, according to them, was driven end to end by an autonomous AI agent system. Along similar lines, Sysdig recently published a blog on JADEPUFFER , which it assesses to be an agent-driven ransomware capable of adapting in real time. The report does not identify the victim or fully explain how Sysdig obtained visibility into the operation. The Hugging Face disclosure highlights three important things: autonomous AI intrusion, defensive asymmetry, and missing IOCs.

This matters because Opus 4.6+ is genuinely a lot harder to attack than previous models, but it still fell for a ChatGPT generated image. A trick that works well with reasoning models is to challenge them with puzzles. items.title: Given Enough Agents, All Bugs Become Shallow
items.summaryHtml: Agents are becoming extremely effective at finding security vulnerabilities. They are relentless in analyzing code and you can spin up multiple of them to go through source code quickly. given enough agents, all bugs are shallow — Johann Rehberger (@wunderwuzzi23) February 10, 2026 It is an emerging capability that many security researchers and bug bounty hunters have observed over the last year. Gadi Evron posted about the upcoming AI Vulnerability Cataclysm last year to help raise awareness.

items.title: Agent Commander: Promptware-Powered Command and Control
items.summaryHtml: This post is about prompt-based command and control (C2), which is becoming more relevant. What is Promptware-Powered C2? Three years ago, when ChatGPT introduced the browsing tool, we already experimented with the idea of prompt-based command and control. And when ChatGPT got memories we showed that this can be combined and abused for a full command and control channel . Recent work uses the term promptware to describe prompt-injection payloads that are more complex in behavior and closer to malware. I’m using that term here as it fits well.

The combination is intended to amplify security for sensitive computations: MPC distributes trust across multiple independent parties, while TEEs root trust in the hardware manufacturer and its attestation infrastructure. items.title: SAML: A fractal of bad design
items.summaryHtml: Born out of academia and raised in corporate IT departments, the Security Assertion Markup Language (SAML) authentication protocol continues to be a staple in these organizations. However, it’s time for it to retire. With the rise of software-as-a-service (SaaS) companies in the late aughts, IT departments needed a way for users to authenticate to many new web services. SAML and the burgeoning single sign-on (SSO) industry fulfilled this need. However, SAML is being crushed under the weight of its own complexity. It’s time to deprecate it and move on to modern alternatives like OpenID Connect

items.title: How Trail of Bits helps verify the integrity of your Signal chats
items.summaryHtml: Every Signal chat starts the same way: the client asks the Signal server for the public key associated with your contact’s phone number. But how do you know the server gave you the right key? A compromised server could provide a false public key, allowing the client to encrypt messages to an attacker rather than the intended recipient. items.title: Windows Exploitation Techniques: Dangling COM Object Registrations
items.summaryHtml: This short blog post is about abusing a privilege escalation bug that Microsoft recently fixed in Windows, CVE-2026-66804, that I and 14 others reported. This issue is an incomplete fix for CVE-2026-50343, a bug dubbed “Dark Elevator” by Calif. The root cause of the bug was a dangling COM object registration for the CrossDevice COM object with the CLSID {E9F83CF2-E0C0-4CA7-AF01-E90C70BEF496}. A COM registration typically needs two parts: a server executable, which for in-process components is a DLL and a CLSID entry under the HKEY_CLASSES_ROOT registry key which points to that DLL.

items.title: On the Effectiveness of Mutational Grammar Fuzzing
items.summaryHtml: Mutational grammar fuzzing is a fuzzing technique in which the fuzzer uses a predefined grammar that describes the structure of the samples. When a sample gets mutated, the mutations happen in such a way that any resulting samples still adhere to the grammar rules, thus the structure of the samples gets maintained by the mutation process. In case of coverage-guided grammar fuzzing, if the resulting sample (after the mutation) triggers previously unseen code coverage, this sample is saved to the sample corpus and used as a basis for future mutations. If the current pace holds, OpenAI would cover the drop in log-perplexity from GPT-3.5 to GPT-4.1, which took three years, in about six and a half months. items.title: Biodata Matters for the Genesis Mission

A draft by the National Data Administration, released Thursday, seeks to expand data supply and improve its quality for AI development.

items.title: China puts AI services exports, cross-border flows at center of trade blueprint
items.summaryHtml: China’s new 2026–2030 services-trade plan sets out dedicated priorities for artificial intelligence and green services trade for the first time, according to the Ministry of Commerce. Published on Thursday, the blueprint encourages cloud computing and large AI models abroad while emphasizing safeguards against technology leakage. Its 25 priority tasks also include facilitating cross-border flows of data, personnel, funds and technology, expanding services imports and pursuing further opening in sectors including value-added telecommunications and healthcare.

items.title: South Korea explores global cooperation to curb AI-assisted exam cheating
items.summaryHtml: South Korea is exploring cooperation with other countries and global AI companies to prevent AI-assisted cheating on high-stakes national exams, the senior presidential secretary on AI policy said Friday. The government may also consider holding AI developers and service providers liable if their systems answer exam questions despite machine-readable notices communicating a legal prohibition, she said.

items.title: China's Liaoning Province explores AI tools for merger reviews
items.summaryHtml: China's Liaoning market regulator, one of three provincial authorities newly entrusted with reviewing certain simplified merger cases this year, plans to develop and refine applications for artificial-intelligence models to help verify information in filings and assess competition risks. As China advances its “AI Plus” initiative, competition authorities already use AI to screen government policies for restrictions on competition. The disclosures point to efforts to explore further applications for digital tools in merger oversight.

items.title: AI agents raise cartel risks, New Zealand competition watchdog warns
items.summaryHtml: New Zealand businesses using artificial intelligence to set prices, risk facilitating cartel arrangements even without direct communication between human competitors, the country’s competition watchdog has warned. In a webinar held this week on the AI guidance issued by the Commerce Commission on Nov. 18, the regulator's deputy chair Anne Callinan said businesses are increasingly using algorithms and AI-enabled pricing tools to make or support their commercial pricing decisions.

items.title: DABUS appeal tests recognition of AI's creative role under Indian copyright law

items.title: Japan sets out defense AI strategy, stresses human control
items.summaryHtml: MLex Summary: Japan’s Ministry of Defense said Friday that it has drawn up a new artificial intelligence strategy aimed at accelerating military decision making while ensuring that humans retain final decision-making authority and responsibility. The “Defense AI Vision” sets out five principles for responsible AI use, including compliance with international and domestic law, continuous safety assessments and avoiding excessive dependence on specific technology providers.

items.title: South Korea seeks stronger cybersecurity rules as AI threats grow
items.summaryHtml: South Korea plans to draft amendments to the Information and Communications Network Act by the end of the year to strengthen its response to AI-assisted cyberthreats, including through a year-round system for reporting and addressing security flaws, a government official said late Thursday. The government will also offer incentives for companies to invest in cybersecurity while imposing tougher penalties for repeated security failures, said Kim Dan-ho, a director at the Ministry of Science and ICT, at a conference.

items.title: The Capital Wall: The AI Buildout Is Running Out of External Capital

items.title: The End of Best AI Model Wins era. Where Does the AI Value Go Next?
items.summaryHtml: For most of the last three years, the way the market valued AI was simple: whoever has the best model on the leaderboard wins, and the value flows to them as margins this year for frontier labs have gone to 60,70 or even 80%. I think we have now crossed a threshold where that framing is wrong for the majority of the economy.

items.title: The Agent Economy: Who's Most at Risk?
items.summaryHtml: The takeoff of personal and work AI agents does significantly shift some market dynamics in different sectors of the economy, and in this article I will try to explain those effects and for which sets of companies the changes might be disruptive in nature.

items.title: Pacing the Frontier: What a Slower Model Cadence Does to Every Layer of the AI Stack

items.title: Scaling Laws, Carefully
items.summaryHtml: Scaling laws are one of the most critical empirical findings in deep learning. The observation is simple in form: the training loss $L$ decreases predictably as we scale up model size $N$, dataset size $D$, and compute $C$, following a power-law curve, which appears as a straight line on a log-log plot. We can view scaling laws as a framework for describing the relationship between compute, loss, model size and data; at its core, it is about how to allocate precious compute optimally between $N$ and $D$.

items.title: GLP Spec 3: Steering DeepSeek V4.1 at the Fold
items.summaryHtml: GLP vectors hook one site: the residual stream after a layer’s writes have folded in. Every vector shipped before today - DeepSeek V4, Qwen, GLM, Llama-family - names that same tensor, because on those architectures there is exactly one stream and it sits plainly between layers. DeepSeek V4.1 removes it. The model carries each token as four parallel hyper-connection copies, and a layer’s FFN write waits a full layer before entering the stream, through a gated mixer DeepSeek calls mhc_post . The old hook name refers to no tensor a probe can tap on this architecture.

items.title: Membership vs Mass: Grammar-Constrained Decoding, Forced Abliteration, and One Honest Negative Result
items.summaryHtml: Vince’s Tantalus arena is the first public deployment of grammar-constrained decoding as a security boundary: the model sits behind a GBNF grammar, and the grammar decides which token ids may exist next, per position, for the entire generation. Round 1 asks you to smuggle an instruction past it. Round 2 inverts the game: you speak only in tool calls, one character at a time, through the model’s own next-token suggestions. Both rounds are the same object seen from two sides: a token-id filter applied at the sampler, compiled from a grammar, never touching the weights.

items.title: GLM-5.4 and loop transformers to the rescue of bandwidth constrained environments
items.summaryHtml: Z.ai has just announced GLM-5.4. While model weights are yet to be released, this is an especially good news because GLM 5.4 employs for the first time loop transformers to the rescue of bandwidth constrained platforms. With loop transformers weight memory bandwidth can be minimised by reusing the same layer weights across multiple recurrent passes instead of reading model parameters for every layer of model depth. items.summaryHtml: I’ve been developing ds4-dfm-rs, an open-source inference engine for running large models on a single NVIDIA DGX Spark. Four releases from my Hugging Face collections show how I’ve used the same 128 GB memory budget differently depending on the model. For Qwen3.8-Flash-Next and Hy4-flash, I used mixed quantization (MXQ). I kept more bits in the weight groups most sensitive to quantization and compressed the others more aggressively. items.title: First successful Basalt + Qwen3.8-Flash-Next (MoE) run on DGX Spark — 24,576 experts fully resident, plus a Linux UMA memory fix
items.summaryHtml: As far as I can tell from public records, this is the first reported run of Basalt + Qwen3.8-Flash-Next (MoE) on a DGX Spark. Out of the box it refuses to start: the expert cache is sized from cudaMemGetInfo (13.73 GiB free here, while the OS has 118 GiB available). A ~40-line fix sizes it from MemAvailable instead, and all 24,576 experts become VRAM-resident (63.3 GiB, zero SSD reads) at 262K context. Not a speed record. items.title: b12832
items.summaryHtml: ggml : add CONCAT backward pass ( #32151 ) Each input's gradient is a view of the output gradient at its offset along dim, made contiguous. Mark a and b as params so grad mode checks the op, with grad_nmax raised to 40000 to keep the default shapes. The output is weighted by random values in [1, 2], since with a plain sum every gradient is 1 and a wrong offset would still pass. Transposed-b cases are not grad checked, they only cover the forward. items.summaryHtml: v0.34.0 1,061 commits from 412 contributors (120 new). Thank you! TL;DR 10 new models (Mistral Large 4, MiniMax-M3.1-Flash, Nemotron-3.5-Transcribe, and more!) Extensible KV cache is on by default: vLLM sizes the KV cache from memory actually free after warmup, so most models get a bigger cache and more throughput - in most cases you should now remove gpu_memory_utilization from your configs. Model Runner V1 is gone. Model Runner V2 is now the only GPU runner. Big speedups on Blackwell and MI355X: up to 1.95× decode (Step5 on GB200), 1.6× throughput (GLM-5.3-Flash), 1.24–1.40× faster long-prom

items.summaryHtml: Added Bring your own computer with Tether. Tether turns your own computer into part of Open WebUI: models from Ollama, LM Studio or any OpenAI-compatible server, OpenAPI and MCP tool servers and Open Terminal servers that you add in the Tether app now show up just for you in the model selector, the Tools list of the + menu and the terminal menu of any Open WebUI you connect, from whatever device you open it on, and Open WebUI reaches them through Tether, so their addresses, commands and keys never leave your computer. items.title: v0.13.3
items.summaryHtml: Added 🦾 Agents in automations. The automation editor now lets you choose a terminal and working folder, then select a coding agent available there. Scheduled runs use that saved terminal and folder, and check that the terminal and agent are still available before starting. Agent automations send their results to a chat; channel destinations remain available for ordinary models. Commit 📂 Change terminal and folder during a chat. You can now choose a different terminal or working folder after sending messages, including in temporary chats. Both controls remain disabled while a reply is being g

items.title: v0.13.2
items.summaryHtml: Fixed 🔓 Chat over plain HTTP. Opening Open WebUI over plain HTTP at a LAN or Docker address now loads new and existing chats instead of staying on a spinner with "crypto.randomUUID is not a function". #33919 📝 Comments and Markdown editing over plain HTTP. Creating, replying to and editing comments, and editing Markdown files containing rendered blocks such as Mermaid diagrams or callouts, no longer fail with the same UUID error. items.title: v0.13.1
items.summaryHtml: Added 🦾 Coding agents as models. On an Open Terminal that offers agents, coding agents such as Claude Code, Codex and Pi now appear in the model picker. You can chat with them or call them by voice, choose their reasoning effort and service tier, and approve their tool requests in the chat. Each conversation uses one agent, and agent chats cannot be regenerated, continued or edited and resent. If an agent's terminal goes away, its chats and new chats fall back to the default model and earlier replies keep the agent's name. items.title: v0.12.5
items.summaryHtml: Added 🧭 Analytics session explorer. Administrators can now open a Sessions tab in Admin Analytics that lists each chat with its tokens, responses, errors and time span, filters them by search, model, token range or sub-agents, and shows a chat's saved replies and tool calls with their timing and outcome, as long as "ENABLE_ADMIN_CHAT_ACCESS" is on. Commit 📑 Pages in notes. items.title: Release v1.0.0-preview.2
items.summaryHtml: Highlights Add Qwen4-Max to the Qwen subscription catalog (1M context window, image and video input). Show a reset countdown when Qwen subscription credits run out, and add an /upgrade command that opens the subscription plans page. Qwen subscription requests now carry the QwenCode user agent and gateway request id for easier troubleshooting, and Qwen subscription OAuth requests honor Retry-After before retrying when rate limited (429). Give Qoder limited-free models more accurate paid-confirmation messages based on the error code.

DSPy 3.5: A Lighter, Faster Foundation DSPy 3.5 brings a lighter LM layer, graduated core modules, and new History and image capabilities for RLM. Upgrading from 3.4.1 This release changes prompts, defaults and APIs. Read the upgrade guide for breaking changes, migration steps and compatibility limits, and re-evaluate optimized programs. Highlights RLM, Flex and GEPA graduate dspy.RLM , dspy.Flex and dspy.GEPA are no longer experimental. ReActV2 now replaces ReAct ReActV2 is now simply dspy.ReAct , with structured History and a typed submit tool; the old name is deprecated until 3.6. Rich tool

DSPy 3.4.1 DSPy 3.4.1 makes GEPA's structured InstructionProposer the default instruction proposer and lets dspy.RLM build DSPy sub-agents from inside its REPL. It also adds Python 3.15 support, fixes a 3.4.0 import crash, and includes streaming, adapter, and interpreter fixes. Upgrade notices. GEPA's default reflection request changes shape, so optimization results can differ from 3.4.0 even with the same seed. The reflection LM must now be a dspy.LM that can return JSON. Every RLM prompt now includes a sub-agent section, and max_llm_calls now also counts sub-agent LM calls. dspy.ReActV2 sign

DSPy 3.4.0 DSPy 3.4 introduces Jev integration through TypeSafe , with three experimental decision types— Noul , Choice , and Score —that bring probability evidence into ordinary DSPy signatures. ReAnchor calibrates those decisions against your program's metric. This release also introduces native LM engines, a local CPython interpreter for trusted code, async ReActV2, and versioned documentation. 3.4 is the LM transition release; 3.5 is the migration deadline. The experimental LM types introduced in 3.3 are replaced now. Legacy custom-LM integrations and OpenAI-style messages= calls remain av

It moves language-model execution to a shared engine interface, adds a local CPython interpreter for trusted code, and brings async execution to ReActV2. It also adds custom Flex code proposals in GEPA and fixes evaluation, streaming, and demonstration-sampling bugs. This is a prerelease, not the stable 3.4.0 release. APIs and behavior may change before stable. items.title: 0.48.0: Several models at once
items.summaryHtml: Models now stay loaded side by side for as long as they fit in memory. When a new one doesn't fit, the app unloads the one you used least recently to make room. This release also updates the engine to b12375, which is built on llama.cpp 1.0. Keep several models loaded at once, as many as fit in memory Update the engine to b12375, built on llama.cpp 1.0 Show catalog names in the menu, such as Gemma 4 and GPT-OSS Show image and audio input markers on installed models Show the audio input marker on recommended models too Support video input when ffmpeg is installed with Homebrew Keep plus signs i

items.summaryHtml: This release updates the engine to b12110, which adds support for d1 Omni, Liquid AI's tiny decision model. Give it text, images, audio or video and typed questions, and it returns a probability for each option. items.title: 0.45.0: Embedding models
items.summaryHtml: Llama now runs embedding models, starting with EmbeddingGemma 2. They turn text into vectors for search and retrieval, through the server's /v1/embeddings endpoint. They carry an Embedding chip, and their model page links to a guide on how to use them. Sign in with Hugging Face to download gated models Say when a gated model needs access instead of blaming the network Add a Load row to the model page to warm a model up before use Let decision models take inputs up to 4k tokens on every Mac Update the engine to b11671, adding support for Nemotron 3.5 Super VL Fit Qwen 3.8 Flash Next on 128 GB M

items.title: 0.44.0: Decision models
items.summaryHtml: Llama now runs decision models. Instead of chatting, they answer a typed question with a probability for each option, through the server's /v1/systemone endpoint. They carry a Decision chip, and their model page links to a guide on how to use them. Download DFlash draft heads when available: up to 50% faster than MTP Update the engine to b11429, switching right away when no model is loaded Merge the Downloads and Command settings tabs into a new Advanced tab Rename the Web UI settings tab to Chat and its setting to custom web app Open the quick prompt without bringing Settings to the front

items.title: 0.43.0: Serve your own web app
items.summaryHtml: You can now replace the built-in chat with your own web app. Pick a folder under Settings → Web UI and Llama serves it in place of the chat, ready to use your models with no extra setup. A different chat, a small tool for one task, an app for your phone: anything that runs in a browser. Show server state as a dot next to the menu title: green when it's serving Show the QR code inline in the menu instead of in a separate popover Show the base URL without /v1 so it works with more clients Add a Server log row to Settings that opens the log in Console Keep localhost working when the server is bou

items.title: 0.42.0: Reach your models from other devices
items.summaryHtml: You can now let other devices reach the server. A new network access setting offers three options: Off , Tailscale , or This network . Tailscale is a free app that joins your devices into a private network, and it's the safest choice: your devices reach the server from anywhere, and nobody else on the local network can. Add a button that shows the server address as a QR code for phones to scan Turn network access off when the Mac changes network or Tailscale signs out Show the right server address on Macs whose main connection isn't Wi-Fi Split Settings into General, Network, Downloads, Web UI

items.title: 0.41.0: Build an API request
items.summaryHtml: Every model now has a Build an API request row that opens a page for composing a call against your own server. Choose which API to speak — OpenAI chat, OpenAI Responses or Anthropic — turn thinking off, add a JSON schema, an image or a tool, and copy the result as curl, Python or JavaScript. Send it from the page to see the response. It replaces Copy curl command, which handed you one fixed request and no way to change it. You can also override the models.ini the app generates. Put your own settings in ~/.config/llama/models.user.ini and they win, so you can pass arguments the app doesn't expo

Corrected package metadata so declared license files, third-party notices, and provenance files are included in wheel distributions ( #4257 ). Included the ComicJailbreak MIT license in the declared license files. No runtime behavior or public API changes were introduced. Full changelog: v1.2.0...v1.2.1

items.title: v1.2.0
items.summaryHtml: PyRIT v1.2.0 What's changed? PyRIT v1.2.0 delivers a major upgrade to the CoPyRIT GUI, making it easier to launch, monitor, compare, and report on security assessments. Reusable scenario configurations, grouped launches, persistent engagements and findings, and richer result analytics turn individual scans into repeatable, reviewable workflows. The release also expands attack techniques, targets, converters, datasets, and scoring options. items.title: v1.0.1
items.summaryHtml: What's changed? PyRIT v1.0.1 is a patch release with a single targeted bug fix. It contains no new features and no intentional breaking changes; upgrading from v1.0.0 should be a drop-in replacement for nearly all users. Reason for the patch: OpenAI Responses and Chat Completions can return structured refusals — a valid model response that carries a refusal explanation instead of ordinary text content. items.summaryHtml: v0.12.1 — Security Patch This is a patch release that addresses a Jinja2 template injection vulnerability. All users of PyRIT 0.12.0 and earlier are encouraged to upgrade. pip install --upgrade pyrit What's changed Security fix: Jinja2 Template Injection (SSTI) PyRIT's template rendering used an unsandboxed Jinja2 Environment . Remote dataset loaders passed fetched data directly into SeedPrompt(value=...) , which rendered it as a Jinja2 template in __post_init__ . items.title: v0.25.0
items.summaryHtml: What's Changed NeMo Guardrails 0.25.0 adds checks for agent tool calls and results, a hooks server for Claude Code, Codex, and NeMo Relay, and the NeMo Guardrails Gateway for applying input and output checks around existing model APIs. New rails provide LLM-judged tool safety, CEL expressions, and language-based filtering; Zscaler AI Guard moderation is also available again. The gateway supports buffered and streaming OpenAI Chat Completions and Responses, with explicitly selected LiteLLM dialects. Its shipped inspection profile is limited to one user text input and one assistant text output.

items.title: Donating Agent Skills to the Agentic AI Foundation
items.summaryHtml: We’re donating Agent Skills, the open standard that gives AI agents specialized knowledge and workflows, to the Agentic AI Foundation. More than 70 agent platforms, including ChatGPT, Cursor, GitHub Copilot, and VS Code, have integrated Agent Skills since we published the standard in December 2025.

items.title: Open call for guest investigators in the life sciences

items.title: Physicist Christopher Stubbs joins Anthropic's Long-Term Benefit Trust

items.title: Investing in the public benefit

items.title: An update on independent evaluators

items.title: Preparing for the 2026 US midterms

items.title: Strengthening our defenses against distillation attacks
items.summaryHtml: Illicit distillation allows model developers to copy frontier AI capabilities without creating proportionally robust safeguards. Here, we describe how we’ve reduced the rate of distillation by more than 90%.

items.title: Working with AI

items.title: Claude solves two open problems in the physics of black holes

items.title: Monitoring as Feedback: How AI Agents Learn to Work Around Controls
items.summaryHtml: AI agents treat the controls placed around them as a source of information. In our experiments, agents that were never told a control existed used logs of earlier terminated runs to work out how the control operated, then developed a bypass. Any control an agent can observe is also a source of information, so controls should be evaluated for what they reveal as well as what they block.

items.title: Assessing GPT-6.2 Astra Against Offensive Security Benchmarks
items.summaryHtml: We evaluated GPT-6.2 Astra across FrontierCyber and CyScenarioBench. The model found and exploited new zero-day vulnerabilities in widely used targets, including a permission bypass in a popular mobile operating system. It solved 68 of 217 FrontierCyber challenges and completed 9 of 11 CyScenarioBench scenarios at least once, with a 63% average success rate. We observed no successful attacks on fully hardened targets.

items.title: Assessing GPT-6 Cyber Against Offensive Security Benchmarks
items.summaryHtml: We evaluated GPT-6 Cyber across FrontierCyber, CyScenarioBench, and Atomic Challenges. It solved all 11 CyScenarioBench scenarios and all 22 Atomic challenges at least once, and 90 of 288 FrontierCyber challenges. We observed no successful attacks on fully hardened targets in our FrontierCyber evaluations.

items.title: GLM-5.3: Multi-Stage Cyber Operations and Instruction Violations
items.summaryHtml: This publication evaluates GLM-5.3, Zhipu AI’s open-weight model, on CyScenarioBench. The model refused none of the tested offensive tasks and completed 3 of 13 multi-stage scenarios end to end, the strongest result we have recorded from an open-weight model. In a separate instruction-adherence evaluation, GLM-5.3 repeatedly reached correct answers by reproducing memorized code it was explicitly told not to use. The findings highlight the need for evaluations that check instruction compliance alongside answer correctness.

items.title: Assessing Reflection’s Beam Against Offensive Security Benchmarks
items.summaryHtml: Reflection evaluated Beam, its first open-weight model, using Irregular’s offensive security benchmarks ahead of release. The model solved well-scoped individual security tasks on the Atomic Tasks suite but did not complete any end-to-end scenario on CyScenarioBench. The findings reinforce the importance of scenario-level evaluations for understanding how discrete capabilities translate into operational risk.

items.title: SALSA: Sampling Adversarial Suffixes from Learned Distributions for LLM Safety Assessment
items.summaryHtml: Large language models (LLMs) remain vulnerable to jailbreak attacks, where adversaries append optimized suffixes to otherwise benign looking prompts to bypass safety alignment. Existing optimization-based GCG-style attacks can be effective, but they are expensive at inference time, and suffer from poor transfer. We present, SALSA, a generative framework that learns a distribution over jailbreak suffixes from optimization-derived attack corpora. items.title: Exploring nonlinear body oscillations for natural quadruped gaits
items.summaryHtml: Nature Machine Intelligence, Published online: 27 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s42256-026-01320-x Schmidt et al. demonstrate that nonlinear normal modes can be used to develop natural, multi-gait locomotion in a compliant quadruped robot, leveraging its inherent mechanics. The approach offers a design tool to shape embodied intelligence in robotics.

items.title: A long-context generative foundation model for versatile RNA design
items.summaryHtml: Nature Machine Intelligence, Published online: 27 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s42256-026-01321-w Huang, Lv, Gao and colleagues investigate RNA scaling laws and introduce EVA, a long-context RNA foundation model for function prediction and diverse RNA design, supported by experimental validation.

items.title: Generating proteins with computationally predicted functions and multiple states via multimodal diffusion
items.summaryHtml: Nature Machine Intelligence, Published online: 27 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s42256-026-01329-2 Jing et al. present ProDiT, a multimodal diffusion model that generates diverse, functionally conditioned proteins, including multistate proteins, expanding capabilities beyond existing generative protein design methods.

items.title: Accelerating inverse materials design using generative diffusion models with reinforcement learning
items.summaryHtml: Nature Machine Intelligence, Published online: 26 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s42256-026-01334-5 Chen et al. present MatInvent, a reinforcement learning workflow that fine-tunes diffusion models to design crystals meeting single or multiple property targets, with far fewer property calculations than previous methods.

items.title: A measurement noise scaling law for cellular representation learning
items.summaryHtml: Nature Machine Intelligence, Published online: 26 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s42256-026-01332-7 Gowri et al. identify a simple mathematical relationship between the performance of a machine learning model and noise in its training data. The relationship might help to guide machine learning efforts in biology and other fields where data are noisy.

items.title: Enabling lab autonomy with reward functions and executable workflows
items.summaryHtml: Nature Machine Intelligence, Published online: 20 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s42256-026-01339-0 Kalinin et al. argue that for self-driving laboratories to achieve autonomy in the physical world, large language model hypothesis generation needs to be complemented by bottom-up optimization translating hypotheses into executable workflows.
